rows.speaker: proponents of taṣawwuf
rows.claim: The author says many, especially Sufis, cite morally effective stories without examining their text or chain of narration.
rows.anchor: especially the proponents of taṣawwuf do not, in principle, give any importance to investigation of chain of narration

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi argues the story is historically implausible: loud revelry in Madinah would have been heard by ʿUmar in the empire’s centre.
rows.anchor: quite improbable that a person in Madī nah and that too in the times of the caliph ‘Umar

rows.speaker: Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet says Satan recoils from ʿUmar’s path, which Islahi treats as further evidence against the story’s plausibility.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) is reported to have said that Satan coils away from the path treaded by ‘Umar (rta)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story would imply ʿUmar did not know the rules against entering by scaling walls and requiring permission and greetings from outside, returning after three refusals.
rows.anchor: not allowed to enter houses by scaling walls and it was necessary to seek permission by offering salutations from outside

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the tale is implausible because ʿUmar neither ordered governors to stop investigating nor ceased such inquiries himself; historical accounts show continued inspection.
rows.anchor: there are numerous incidents recorded in history which show that his administrators continued to pry and be inquisitive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accepting the story would give even grave crimes committed at home immunity from police or caliphal entry, leaving only a gentle admonition.
rows.anchor: if in an Islamic state some people consume liquor in the confines of their houses, indulge in lecherous activities with women of loose character

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi concludes that the widely cited account of ʿUmar entering a home is absolutely unreliable.
rows.anchor: this narrative, in my opinion, is absolutely unreliable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An Islamic government must protect citizens’ character as well as public order and may investigate a suspicion, while observing moral and legal limits; abusive investigation is criminal before God and harms innocents.
rows.anchor: it has the right to pry wherever there is a doubt; however, exercising each right has some moral and legal restrictions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Good-intentioned inquiry aimed at helping the poor who preserve their self-respect is virtuous; believers should seek them out rather than wait for them to beg.
rows.anchor: the self respecting poor and to try to take the initiative in reaching them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People should address suspected clandestine conduct that threatens life, honour, property, or public security by seeking reform or help from those able to intervene.
rows.anchor: People should try to reform him and if it is not possible for them, then help should be sought from those who are in a position to do so

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi illustrates communal responsibility with ship passengers: one who sees a passenger boring a hole must take away the axe or all will drown.
rows.anchor: This responsibility has been taught to the believers by giving the example of the passengers of a ship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For a private fault, counsel the person if able; otherwise conceal it, since God conceals those who conceal others’ faults. If the fault is contagious, curb it as the Prophet directs.
rows.anchor: he should ignore his fault and conceal it. God also hides the flaws of people who hide the faults of others

rows.speaker: Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: The Prophet’s directive to curb evil applies when a fault is contagious rather than merely personal.
rows.anchor: follow the directive of the Prophet (sws) which relates to curbing evil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports about concealing a Muslim’s sins must be read in their occasion and context; they do not mean ignoring other people’s wrongdoing or concealing every fault.
rows.anchor: people do not reflect on the occasion and background of Qur’ ānic verses and prophetic narratives

rows.speaker: Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: A Prophetic report requires a person who sees evil to stop it by hand, then by speech if unable; if neither is possible, they must regard it as evil in the heart, the lowest level of faith.
rows.anchor: a person sees an evil he should curb it with his hands; if this is not possible, he should try to curb it

rows.speaker: Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: The report identifies rejection in the heart as the last available response and says no faith remains below that level.
rows.anchor: he should regard it to be evil in his heart; there is no level of faith below it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Context resolves the apparent tension: ordinary discourtesy, such as standing to urinate, may be excused, counselled against, or discreetly concealed if one cannot counsel.
rows.anchor: If a person is urinating while standing, one can ignore him thinking that he might have some excuse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Serious threats such as a liquor factory, drugs, hidden weapons, or a brothel must be reported to authorities rather than concealed as a private sin.
rows.anchor: if it is known about a person that he has set up a liquor manufacturing plant in his house

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Invoking God’s promise to conceal sins as a reason to hide such grave wrongdoing is wishful thinking and could lead its adherents to lose faith.
rows.anchor: this, in my opinion, is mere wishful thinking. People who adopt this attitude might end up losing their faith

rows.speaker: these people
rows.claim: Some reconcile duties to investigate narrators, testify, curb evil, and advise Muslims with the ban on backbiting by treating them as strategic exceptions; Islahi rejects that framing.
rows.anchor: they reconciled them by saying that all these things came under the head of backbiting but they have been declared lawful because of strategy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Investigating transmitters, giving true testimony, curbing evil, and sincere counsel are religious obligations, not merely strategic permissions.
rows.anchor: they have in fact been made obligatory by it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says scrutiny of transmitters underpins the discipline of the sharīʿah.
rows.anchor: The discipline of sharī‘ah is based on investigation of narrators

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bearing witness is a responsibility for which this Muslim community was established in the world.
rows.anchor: bearing witness is the responsibility of this ummah for which it had been instituted in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The community’s life and sustenance depend on its responsibility to curb evil.
rows.anchor: life and sustenance of this ummah has been made dependent by God on the responsibility of curbing evil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Well-wishing is required both by Muslim fraternity and by faith; Islahi says this has already been stated in the sūrah.
rows.anchor: being well-wishers of Muslims is not only a requirement of being in the fraternity it is also a requirement of faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Backbiting has a specific scope; its prohibition does not block religious obligations and does not need a strategic exception to permit them.
rows.anchor: Its prohibition in no way stops or interferes in religious obligations, nor under a strategy does it need to be legalized to carry them out

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says hadith scholars, revivalists, and reformers have not allowed strategic legalization of backbiting; only those who turn the sharīʿah into a tool of strategy would need it.
rows.anchor: Neither have the scholars of Ḥadīth allowed it nor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah’s closing verses expose the inner condition of people whose conduct was condemned in its opening five verses, completing its movement from public manners to the underlying malady.
rows.anchor: Coming up are the closing verses of the sūrah in which the inner personalities of people whose attitude was condemned in the first five verses are revealed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tribes around Madīnah embraced Islam when its power grew, but their distance from the centre left them inadequately trained.
rows.anchor: certain tribes which lived around Mad īnah had entered the fold of the Muslims when they saw the rising might of Islam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those tribes conceitedly thought that accepting faith without war was a favour to the Prophet and Islam, which helps explain their failure to observe proper manners.
rows.anchor: they harboured the conceited notion that they had done a great favour to the Prophet (sws) and to Islam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The initial rebukes address everyone generally so those with such faults can reform; at the end, the tribes are named and their malady exposed because faith cannot flourish while it remains.
rows.anchor: Now, here at the end, they are addressed by name and their real malady has been exposed so that they turn towards its remedy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects Orientalist attempts to reorder the sūrahs, insisting that the Qur’an’s arrangement is divine and prophetic; the Orientalists claim their sequence is more meaningful and removes a supposedly haphazard order.
rows.anchor: They have rearranged them claiming that this new arrangement is more meaningful and better arranges the Book of God and rids it of the haphazard sequence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi notes that some Muslim countries publish Qur’an editions using readings other than the familiar mutawātir reading of Ḥafṣ.
rows.anchor: not on the conventional and well known mutawātir reading (the reading of Ḥafṣ)
